claims.text: The degree of simultaneity in precursor reduction governs whether noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles form as a homogeneous single phase or segregate into multiple domains.
Aligning the reduction rates of all precursors within a narrow window produces co-nucleation.
Co-nucleation and atomic mixing produce a homogeneous alloy.
Large differences among precursor reduction rates cause sequential nucleation.
Sequential nucleation leads to phase separation or elemental segregation.
The initial mixed precursor solution exhibits a spread of intrinsic reduction potentials.
A coordinating ligand can selectively slow the reduction kinetics of the fastest-reducing precursor.
Ligand coordination slows electron transfer to the fastest-reducing precursor.
Slowing the fastest-reducing precursor synchronizes its reduction with that of slower precursors.
Synchronized reduction increases temporal overlap among nucleation events and generates co-nucleated nuclei containing all metal species.
Simultaneous nucleation traps all metals in a single mixed phase.
Ligand-treated synthesis will yield nanoparticles with uniform elemental distributions and low variance in per-particle composition.
Untreated synthesis will exhibit asynchronous reduction and produce core-shell structures or segregated domains.
The proposed mechanism applies to wet-chemical solution-phase reduction of noble-metal precursors when ligand coordination can tune their reduction behavior.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to solid-state thermal mixing methods such as carbothermal shock.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to non-noble metals with irreversible precursor chemistries.
Individual ligand-metal interactions may introduce additional variability in compositional uniformity.
